The diagnostic value of coronary computed tomography angiography–derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT)
in stable coronary artery disease is well established. The prognostic value of predicting future cardiovascular events is less
clear, as studies are limited by small populations, variable measurement points, composite outcomes, and short follow-up.
A nationwide cohort of coronary computed tomography angiography with 3-year follow-up was used to examine
the association between FFR-CT measurements and future cardiovascular events.
Patients receiving coronary computed tomography angiography and clinically indicated FFR-CT analysis (HeartFlow)
for stable coronary artery disease between 2017 and 2020 at 27 sites across England were included. Lowest per-patient
stenosis-specific and distal vessel FFR-CT measurements were related to individual outcomes of myocardial infarction (MI),
cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and revascularization. FFR-CT measurements were divided into subgroups to
investigate for a gradient of risk: normal FFR-CT (>0.8), borderline (0.71–0.8), reduced (0.51–0.7), and severely reduced
In total, 7836 patients aged 63 (56.0–71.0), 37.4% women, underwent FFR-CT analysis. Stenosis-specific FFR-CT

CT discordance was common (36.4%), but when stenosis-specific FFR-CT was normal, event rates were low (1.5% at 3
years for MI or cardiovascular death).
FFR-CT is associated with the individual outcomes of MI, cardiovascular death, and all-cause death independent
of risk factors and stenosis severity, with lower FFR-CT values associated with worse outcomes. Reduced and severely

Therefore, FFR-CT is recommended for use in the

However, the evidence to date is based
on small numbers, composite outcomes, or a limited
follow-up period. It therefore remains uncertain whether
FFR-CT offers incremental prognostic value beyond tra
ditional risk factors and stenosis severity. This question
is particularly relevant given the ongoing debate over
whether myocardial ischemia is itself prognostic or sim
ply a downstream marker of anatomical CAD severity.
Interpreting the FFR-CT evidence to date is further
used across studies. Stenosis-specific FFR-CT (2 cm

large nationwide cohort with sufficient clinical events
and follow-up to determine the association between
FFR-CT and individual cardiovascular outcomes, which
FFR-CT measurement has the greatest prognostic value,
and whether these variables add incremental prognostic
information beyond traditional cardiovascular risk factors

Continuous variables are reported as mean (±SD) or median
Between-group differences were assessed by ANOVA for
continuous variable and a Cochran-Armitage trend test for cat
egorical differences, with the “no stenosis-specific value” group
representing the category with the least disease. Time to first
event was calculated using Kaplan-Meier methodology from
the time of the CCTA. Cox proportional regression was used
to determine the univariable hazard ratio (HR) for individual
clinical outcomes post FFR-CT, and the proportional hazard
assumptions were tested using Shoenfeld residuals. Fine-Grey
modeling was performed to account for competing risks where
necessary. Multivariable Cox regression models were used to
adjust for patient cardiovascular risk factors (age, sex, hyperten
sion, diabetes, dyslipidemia) and the Coronary Artery Disease
Reporting and Data System (CAD-RADS) score. Models were
developed to determine the performance of baseline risk fac
combined end point of MI and cardiovascular death. Model per
formance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic
analysis with Harrell’s C statistic and the Akaike information
criterion with the Brier score as a measure of model calibration.
FFR-CT was entered into an adjusted multivariable model as a
continuous variable to provide an adjusted HR (aHR) per 0.01
unit decrease in stenosis-specific FFR-CT. A restricted cubic
spline curve analysis with 3 knots was performed to assess the
relationship of FFR-CT as a continuous variable to the clinical
outcomes. The 95% CIs are reported, and 2-sided
considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were

This large multicenter study is the first to show that FFR-
CT stratifies risk for the individual outcomes of MI, car
diovascular death, all-cause death, and revascularization
at 3 years. Importantly, this is incremental to clinical risk
factors and coronary stenosis severity. A risk continuum
exists, as lower FFR-CT values are associated with in
crementally worse prognosis, with an optimum stenosis-
specific threshold of 0.67 for defining increased risk of
future cardiac events. Stenosis-specific and distal-vessel
FFR-CT models performed equivalently in discriminating
outcomes, although stenosis-specific models had better

Prior studies have pointed to the prognostic potential
of FFR-CT in predicting cardiovascular events but have
been limited by small numbers, composite outcomes, and
short follow-up. The largest previous study, from the Dan
ish ADVANCE registry, showed that a positive FFR-CT
was associated with an increased risk of all-cause death
and MI combined out to 7 years of follow-up.

Our observations raise the question as to whether
distal vessel FFR-CT values should be reported, as the
models based on distal-vessel and stenosis-specific
FFR-CT perform similarly. The risk of a “don’t report
distal” approach is that potentially important patient-
specific information is not used, as reduced and severely
reduced distal-vessel values do have an association with
future cardiovascular events and all-cause death. This is
corroborated by invasive studies showing that distal FFR
in the 3 main epicardial vessels predicts major adverse
burden over the entire epicardial coronary artery rather
than specific obstructive stenoses, with lower values
suggesting diffuse disease and worse vascular health.
Indeed, the plaque literature highlights the importance
of total plaque volume across the coronary tree in pre
dicting major adverse cardiovascular events, not just
stenosis severity or presence of ischemia.
it is challenging to disentangle the impact of distal
FFR-CT from an upstream stenosis-specific FFR-CT,
